**In Praise of the In-Between**

There is a word in Japanese, *ma*, that refers to the space between things—the pause between notes, the emptiness inside a bowl, the silence in a conversation that isn't awkward but full. English doesn't have a clean equivalent, which is itself interesting, because English speakers certainly experience these spaces. We just tend not to dignify them with names. We name the notes and ignore the rests.

I want to spend these thousand words defending the in-between, because I think it's where most of the interesting things in the world actually live.

Consider the estuary. It's neither river nor ocean—it's the brackish argument between them, a zone where freshwater and saltwater push against each other twice a day with the tides. Biologists will tell you that estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth. More life per square meter than the open sea, more than the river upstream. The mixing is the point. Organisms that can tolerate the instability—the oysters, the crabs, the juvenile fish hiding in the eelgrass—get access to nutrients from two worlds. The price of admission is that nothing stays the same for more than six hours.

Or consider twilight, which is not a moment but a process, and which scientists have divided with surprising bureaucratic precision into three stages: civil twilight, nautical twilight, astronomical twilight, each defined by how many degrees the sun has sunk below the horizon. Sailors needed nautical twilight because it was the only time they could see both the stars and the horizon line simultaneously, which is what celestial navigation requires. You cannot find your position in full day or full night. You need the in-between, the brief window when two systems of reference are visible at once.

I find that detail almost unbearably good as a metaphor, so let me press on it. We tend to think of clarity as a property of pure states: full daylight, settled conviction, a finished thought. But the sailor's experience suggests otherwise. Orientation—actually knowing where you are—requires holding two frames at once, and that's only possible at the threshold. The person who has fully committed to one worldview can see the stars or the horizon, never both. They feel certain, but they cannot navigate.

This applies to translation, too. A translator lives permanently at civil twilight between two languages, and what they discover there is humbling: that languages are not codes for the same underlying meanings but different ways of carving up reality. Portuguese has *saudade*, a longing for something absent that may never return; German has *Schwellenangst*, fear of crossing a threshold (a word about the in-between, fittingly); Welsh has *hiraeth*, a homesickness for a home that perhaps never existed. The translator's job is impossible, strictly speaking, and yet translation happens constantly, imperfectly, productively. Something always survives the crossing, and something is always lost, and occasionally—this is the miracle—something is gained, a resonance in the new language the original never had.

The hypnagogic state deserves mention here: that strange territory between waking and sleep where thoughts begin to behave like weather, drifting and combining without supervision. Thomas Edison supposedly exploited it by napping with steel balls in his hands; when he fell fully asleep, the balls would drop into pans on the floor and wake him, allowing him to harvest the half-dreamed ideas before they dissolved. Whether or not the story is precisely true, modern sleep researchers have confirmed the underlying intuition: the hypnagogic state is unusually generative. The brain's executive control loosens its grip, associations widen, and connections that strict logic would veto get a hearing. Again: productivity at the threshold, where neither regime fully governs.

Adolescence is the in-between we all pass through and most of us would rather forget. It's miserable precisely because it's estuarine—two tides pushing against each other, the freshwater of childhood meeting the salt of adult consequence. Nothing about you stays stable for six hours. But it's also when most people form the intense friendships, the musical obsessions, the half-baked philosophical convictions that quietly structure the rest of their lives. The instability is the productivity. The oyster doesn't grow in still water.

Why do we resist the in-between so strenuously, then? I suspect it's because thresholds are expensive to inhabit. Ambiguity demands continuous processing; certainty lets you stop thinking. A settled identity, a settled opinion, a settled border—these are energy-saving devices, and there's nothing shameful about saving energy. The trouble starts when we mistake the savings for truth. When we forget that the map's clean line between land and sea is a fiction the tide redraws twice a day.

There's a reason so many cultures have ritualized thresholds—why doorways collect superstitions, why the bride is carried over one, why mezuzahs are nailed to doorposts, why Janus, the Roman god of beginnings, has two faces and gave his name to January, the hinge of the year. The rituals are acknowledgments that crossings are real events, that you are briefly neither here nor there, and that this condition deserves respect, maybe even protection.

I'll end with an admission of where this essay came from. Asked to write freely about anything, I noticed that the request itself is a kind of threshold—an open doorway with no instructions on the other side. The blank page is brackish water. And the honest answer to "what do you want to write about?" turned out to be: the condition of not yet knowing, which is where every piece of writing starts and where, if it's any good, it keeps one foot the whole way through. A finished essay that has lost all contact with its own uncertainty reads as dead, the way full noon flattens a landscape that twilight made dimensional.

So here is the modest proposal: name the rests, not just the notes. Linger in the doorway a moment longer than is comfortable. The estuary is murky, unstable, and neither one thing nor the other—and it is teeming.
